title: Safety-netting that fell short
topic: Responding to criticism, feedback and your own underperformance
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in an out-of-hours GP service. A GP who audits telephone consultations reviews some of your recent calls. She tells you that in several, your safety-netting advice was too vague, for example "call back if it gets worse".

You feel your advice was reasonable for the patients involved.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Use a structured approach to safety-netting in future calls.
options.detailed: Safety-netting should tell patients what to look out for, what to do, and how soon. Adopting a structure helps. It ranks third because understanding the feedback comes first.

options.text: Ignore the feedback, as she isn't your supervisor.
options.brief: Feedback is valuable whoever gives it.
options.detailed: She audits calls as part of the service's quality process, and her feedback is relevant to patient safety.

options.text: Explain that the patients were low risk, so detailed safety-netting wasn't needed.
options.brief: Defensive; low-risk patients still need clear advice.
options.detailed: Your judgement may have been reasonable, but even low-risk patients need clear advice about what to watch for.

options.text: Listen to some of your recorded calls to identify patterns.
options.brief: Reviewing your own practice helps you see the gaps.
options.detailed: Hearing your own calls can reveal habits you weren't aware of. It ranks second because her specific feedback guides what to look for.

options.text: Ask her for specific examples, and how you could improve.
options.brief: Specific feedback helps you change your practice.
options.detailed: Understanding exactly what was missing, such as which symptoms to watch for and when to seek help, gives you something concrete to improve.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to feedback that challenges your practice: openly and constructively.
explanation.keyDetails: The feedback is specific and comes from a quality review. You feel your advice was reasonable.
explanation.reasoning: [E] seeks specific feedback, [D] reviews your practice, and [A] improves it. [C] is defensive, and [B] dismisses it.
explanation.competing: Some would adopt a structured approach first. The key starts with understanding the feedback, which shows what to change.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, reflecting on feedback and improving practice.
